ANNUAL REGULATORY INSPECTION REPORT — HARTFIELD VETERINARY CLINIC
Inspecting authority: Regional Veterinary Practice Board
Lead inspector: Wanjiru Fischer, MRCVS. Accompanying officer: Callum Tanaka.
Practice principal: Dr Nadia Osei. Report author: Wanjiru Fischer.
Inspection dates: 3–4 September. Report issued: 18 September. Reference: RVPB/INS/2289.

SECTION A — PREMISES AND BIOSECURITY
A1. The clinic comprises a reception area, two consulting rooms, one operating theatre, a kennel ward (14 kennels), an isolation ward (3 kennels), and a pharmacy store.
A2. The isolation ward has a dedicated entrance, negative-pressure ventilation tested and certificated on 21 May of the current year, and dedicated PPE stock. Compliant.
A3. The main kennel ward's drainage channel was partially obstructed by bedding debris at the time of inspection; staff cleared it during the visit and the cleaning rota was amended on the spot to include a daily channel check. Recorded as a minor finding, remediated during inspection.
A4. Theatre surfaces, lighting, and scavenging systems: compliant. Anaesthetic machine service certificate dated 2 February, current.

SECTION B — MEDICINES MANAGEMENT
B1. The controlled drugs register was examined for the period 1 January to 31 August. Entries were contemporaneous, witnessed, and reconciled to physical stock on three of four sample dates. On 14 July, the register records 28 remaining ampoules of ketamine while physical stock on 15 July was 27; the discrepancy was investigated internally at the time, attributed to a broken ampoule recorded in the wastage log but not cross-referenced in the register, and corrected by the practice on 16 July with a memorandum entry. The Board's guidance (GN-7, para 4) requires cross-referencing of wastage within the register itself. Recorded as a minor finding; the practice's corrective memorandum is accepted and no further action is required.
B2. Refrigerated medicines: the pharmacy fridge's minimum/maximum thermometer records for the preceding 90 days were complete and within range on all days except 22 July, when a maximum of 9.4 °C was recorded following a power cut; the affected stock was quarantined and returned to the wholesaler, with the returns note on file. Compliant, with the incident handled per protocol.
B3. The dispensary holds a current wholesale dealing authorisation, certificate sighted, expiry 31 March next year.

SECTION C — CLINICAL RECORDS AND CONSENT
C1. Twenty patient records were sampled. Nineteen contained signed consent forms for the procedures performed. One record (feline, dental procedure, 5 June) contained a consent form signed by a person other than the registered owner; the record notes the signer was the owner's adult daughter and that verbal owner consent was obtained by telephone, but the telephone consent was not documented in the record at the time. Standard of Record-Keeping 11 requires contemporaneous documentation of third-party and telephone consent. Recorded as a finding requiring improvement; the practice must audit telephone-consent documentation within 60 days and report the audit outcome to the Board.
C2. Record completeness, legibility, and retention: compliant.

SECTION D — STAFFING AND TRAINING
D1. Staffing levels met the Board's minimum for the caseload in all sampled weeks.
D2. CPD records were current for all veterinary surgeons. One veterinary nurse's CPD record showed 13 hours against the required 15 for the prior cycle; the shortfall was made up in the current cycle and is treated as closed.

SECTION E — COMPLAINTS AND GOVERNANCE
E1. The complaints log shows nine complaints in twelve months, all acknowledged within the required three working days; eight were resolved with a written response within 20 working days. One complaint (billing dispute, logged 2 August) remained open at 32 days at inspection; the practice provided evidence of an agreed extension with the complainant. Compliant.
E2. Clinical governance meetings: minutes sighted for eight of the last twelve months; the Board's expectation is monthly meetings. Recorded as a finding requiring improvement.

SECTION F — SUMMARY OF FINDINGS
F1. Minor findings remediated during inspection: A3.
F2. Minor findings, no further action: B1.
F3. Findings requiring improvement with follow-up: C1 (audit within 60 days), E2 (monthly governance meetings to be evidenced at next inspection).
F4. No findings of serious concern. No referral to the disciplinary committee. The clinic's registration continues unconditionally.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT: The clinic is rated SATISFACTORY. The next routine inspection is due within 36 months of the issue date.

Signed: Wanjiru Fischer, Lead Inspector. Countersigned: Callum Tanaka, Accompanying Officer.
Distribution: Practice principal; Board secretariat; registration file.

MERIDIAN FREIGHT FOUNDATION — COMMUNITY GRANT PROGRAM
Application Section 4: Program Narrative and Appendices
Applicant Organization: Harbor Literacy Project
Primary Contact: Greta Rahman, Executive Director
Application ID: MF-2024-1187
Requested Amount: $75,000
Program Period: September 1 – August 31

---

SECTION 4.1 — ORGANIZATIONAL BACKGROUND

The Harbor Literacy Project (HLP) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded eleven years ago to provide free reading instruction to adults in the harbor district who read below an eighth-grade level. Our mission is straightforward: every adult in our district who wants to read fluently should have a free, patient, and competent place to learn. We serve approximately 340 learners per year with a staff of seven (four full-time, three part-time) and a trained volunteer corps of 118 tutors. Our annual operating budget for the most recent completed fiscal year was $612,000, of which 71% came from foundation grants, 18% from individual giving, 8% from a municipal contract, and 3% from interest income.

HLP operates one main learning center and three satellite sites housed in public library branches. Our flagship program, One-to-One Tutoring, matches each learner with a trained volunteer tutor for two ninety-minute sessions per week. Our second program, Family Reading Nights, is a monthly event series that brings learners' children into the center for shared reading and a free dinner; it served 96 families last year. Our third and newest program, Workplace Words, delivers on-site basic literacy instruction to employees of local firms during paid work hours; it is described in detail in Section 4.3 because this application requests funding primarily for its expansion.

HLP is governed by a nine-member board of directors. Our treasurer, Oren Mensah, has served six years and is a retired hospital finance officer. Our board chair is a former adult learner of this program, a fact of which we are deeply proud.

---

SECTION 4.2 — STATEMENT OF NEED

District census data indicate that approximately 14,000 adults in our service area read below an eighth-grade level. Roughly 6,200 of them read below a third-grade level. The consequences are documented and severe: adults with low literacy are twice as likely to be unemployed, three times as likely to report poor health, and dramatically less likely to read to their children, perpetuating an intergenerational cycle.

Demand for our services exceeds capacity. Our waiting list for One-to-One Tutoring currently stands at 87 adults, with an average wait of five months. We have never advertised the program; every learner arrives by word of mouth or referral from the library system, the workforce center, or the two clinics where we leave brochures.

The workplace dimension of this need is the focus of the present request. Employers in the district — particularly in logistics, food service, and building maintenance — report that basic literacy gaps among entry-level employees create safety risks (misread warning labels, misunderstood equipment instructions), reduce retention, and block promotion of otherwise reliable workers. At the same time, these employees are precisely the adults least able to attend evening classes at our center, because many hold second jobs or have evening childcare responsibilities. Bringing instruction to the workplace, on paid time, removes both barriers at once.

---

SECTION 4.3 — PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: WORKPLACE WORDS EXPANSION

Workplace Words launched three years ago as a pilot with a single employer partner, a commercial laundry. In the pilot year, 22 employees enrolled and 17 completed the nine-month curriculum; completers gained an average of 1.8 grade levels in reading as measured by the standardized assessment we use across all programs. Two years ago we added a second partner, a regional grocery chain's distribution warehouse. Last year, 41 learners enrolled across the two sites and 33 completed.

This application requests $75,000 to expand Workplace Words from two employer partners to five, serving a projected 95 enrolled learners over the twelve-month program period, with a completion target of 75 learners (we budget conservatively at roughly 80% completion, consistent with our three-year average of 79%).

Program design at each site: two cohorts of 8–12 learners; each cohort meets twice weekly for ninety minutes during paid work hours, scheduled at shift boundaries in coordination with the employer. Instruction is delivered by one of our part-time staff instructors, supported by two trained volunteer tutors per cohort. Curriculum is contextualized to the employer's environment — learners practice reading using the actual safety manuals, schedules, and forms of their workplace, which our evaluation data show measurably accelerates gains compared to generic workbooks.

The three prospective new employer partners are named in Appendix B. Letters of intent from all three are included in Appendix C.

Program staff costs account for the majority of the request. The full budget is in Section 4.5.

---

SECTION 4.4 — EVALUATION PLAN

All learners are assessed at intake and at completion using the same standardized adult reading assessment used across our programs. We report: enrollment, completion, average grade-level gain, and — unique to Workplace Words — two employer-reported indicators collected via a structured supervisor survey at six and twelve months: (1) observed safety-incident rates involving cohort members, and (2) internal promotion or wage-progression rates of completers versus a non-enrolled comparison group identified by the employer. In the pilot, completers were promoted at 2.4 times the rate of the comparison group over twelve months.

We will report to the Foundation at six months (mid-year) and at thirteen months (final, one month after program close), using the Foundation's standard report form.

---

SECTION 4.5 — BUDGET NARRATIVE (Summary)

Total program cost for the expansion year: $118,500.

- Staff instructors (part-time, three sites): $54,000
- Volunteer tutor training and coordination: $9,500
- Curriculum materials and assessments: $11,000
- Learner incentives (transit passes, completion certificates, celebration events): $4,000
- Program manager (0.5 FTE, salary and benefits): $32,000
- Evaluation and reporting: $4,500
- Indirect costs (4%): $3,500

Revenue committed or requested:

- This request to the Meridian Freight Foundation: $75,000
- Employer partner contributions (cash, per letters in Appendix C): $21,000 total — $7,000 per site from each of the three new partners
- HLP board-designated reserve allocation: $12,500 — APPROVED by board resolution on the consent agenda of our May board meeting, minuted and available on request
- Individual donor pledge: $10,000 — pledged verbally by a long-standing individual donor at our spring breakfast; written pledge confirmation is pending and expected before program start

The Foundation's guidelines require that applicants demonstrate at least 25% of total program cost from non-Foundation sources that are SECURED at the time of application. We calculate our secured non-Foundation share as follows: employer cash contributions ($21,000, documented by signed letters of intent) plus the board reserve allocation ($12,500, documented by board minutes) equals $33,500, which is 28.3% of the $118,500 total. The verbal $10,000 pledge is NOT included in the secured calculation, per the guidelines' definition of secured funds; we list it transparently as pending.

---

SECTION 4.6 — SUSTAINABILITY

Employer partners pay $7,000 per site in year one; our signed letters commit them to $9,000 per site in year two and $11,000 in year three, reflecting the value they report receiving. At year-three rates, employer contributions plus our municipal contract renewal would cover approximately 85% of ongoing program costs. We will seek renewed foundation support only for the residual and for any further expansion.

---

APPENDIX A — BOARD OF DIRECTORS ROSTER (abbreviated)

Chair: [former program learner; name withheld in this distribution copy]
Treasurer: Oren Mensah, retired hospital finance officer
Secretary: Lena Osei, school librarian (ret.)
Members: six additional members from healthcare, law, education, and the trades

---

APPENDIX B — PROSPECTIVE NEW EMPLOYER PARTNERS

1. A regional food-service commissary employing 210 workers, 0.8 miles from our main center. Site contact: HR director.
2. A building-maintenance contractor employing 140 workers across the district. Site contact: operations manager.
3. A cold-storage logistics facility employing 175 workers. Site contact: Dmitri Lindqvist, shift operations supervisor, who has championed this partnership internally and coordinated the letter of intent.

Note: none of the three new partners is a freight carrier; we approached two freight carriers during planning, but both declined due to pending union contract negotiations. The cold-storage facility is logistics-adjacent but independently owned.

---

APPENDIX C — LETTERS OF INTENT (excerpts)

Excerpt 1 (commissary): "We commit to hosting two cohorts, releasing participating employees with pay for all sessions, and contributing $7,000 in year one..."
Excerpt 2 (building maintenance): "...contribution of $7,000 in year one, rising per the schedule in your proposal..."
Excerpt 3 (cold storage): "...pleased to confirm our $7,000 contribution and paid release time. Dmitri Lindqvist will serve as our program liaison..."

---

APPENDIX D — TIMELINE

September: instructor hiring and site setup at all three new sites; baseline assessments.
October: cohorts begin at all five sites (two existing, three new).
March: mid-year assessments and Foundation interim report.
July: final sessions and completion assessments.
August: program close; employer surveys administered.
September (month 13): final report to the Foundation.

---

APPENDIX E — PRIOR SUPPORT FROM THE MERIDIAN FREIGHT FOUNDATION

HLP has received one prior grant from this Foundation: a $40,000 general operating grant five years ago, fully expended and reported on schedule. Final report accepted; no findings. We did not apply in the intervening years because our program growth was absorbed by two multi-year grants from other funders, both now concluded.

---

CERTIFICATION

I certify that the information in this application is accurate and complete to the best of my knowledge.

Greta Rahman, Executive Director
Date: June 12

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CASCADIA
COUNTY OF HARBORVIEW

GRANITE LOGISTICS, INC., a Cascadia corporation,
    Plaintiff,
v.
SEABROOK UNIVERSITY DEPARTMENT OF MARINE BIOCHEMISTRY, a public research institution; DR. TOMASZ NOVAK, in his official capacity as Laboratory Director; and JONAS KAUR, in his official capacity as Facilities Coordinator,
    Defendants.

Case No. 24-2-08731-6

PLAINTIFF'S FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT, UNJUST ENRICHMENT, AND CONVERSION

COMES NOW the Plaintiff, Granite Logistics, Inc. ("Granite"), by and through its undersigned counsel, and for its First Amended Complaint against Defendants Seabrook University Department of Marine Biochemistry (the "Department"), Dr. Tomasz Novak, and Jonas Kaur (collectively, "Defendants"), alleges as follows:

I. PARTIES

1.1 Plaintiff Granite Logistics, Inc. is a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the State of Cascadia, with its principal place of business in Harborview, Cascadia. Granite is engaged in the business of transporting temperature-sensitive scientific equipment and biological materials.

1.2 Defendant Seabrook University Department of Marine Biochemistry is an academic department of Seabrook University, a public institution of higher education located in Harborview, Cascadia. The Department operates the Coldroom Annex, a research facility at 1140 Pier Street, where the events giving rise to this action occurred.

1.3 Defendant Dr. Tomasz Novak is the Laboratory Director of the Department and is sued in his official capacity only. Dr. Novak signed the Master Transport Services Agreement described below on behalf of the Department.

1.4 Defendant Jonas Kaur is the Facilities Coordinator of the Department and is sued in his official capacity only. Mr. Kaur supervised the loading dock at the Coldroom Annex on the dates at issue.

II. JURISDICTION AND VENUE

2.1 This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to Cascadia law because the amount in controversy exceeds seventy-five thousand dollars ($75,000), exclusive of interest and costs.

2.2 Venue is proper in Harborview County because the contract at issue was to be performed in Harborview County and because the events giving rise to this action occurred in Harborview County.

III. FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

A. The Master Transport Services Agreement

3.1 On or about January 12, 2023, Granite and the Department entered into a Master Transport Services Agreement (the "Agreement"), a true and correct copy of which is attached hereto as Exhibit A and incorporated herein by reference.

3.2 Under Section 2.1 of the Agreement, Granite agreed to provide refrigerated transport of scientific equipment and biological samples between the Department's Coldroom Annex and various field research stations along the Cascadia coast.

3.3 Under Section 4.2 of the Agreement, the Department agreed to pay Granite's invoices within forty-five (45) days of receipt. Section 4.4 of the Agreement provides that invoices not paid within forty-five (45) days shall accrue interest at a rate of one and one-half percent (1.5%) per month.

3.4 Under Section 7.1 of the Agreement, Granite's liability for loss of or damage to cargo is limited to the declared value stated on the bill of lading, unless the Department purchased supplemental declared-value coverage at the time of booking.

3.5 Under Section 7.3 of the Agreement, any claim for damage to cargo must be submitted in writing within fourteen (14) calendar days of delivery, accompanied by photographic documentation of the damage taken at the time of delivery. Section 7.3(c) provides a narrow exception: where damage is latent and could not reasonably be discovered at delivery, the written claim period is extended to thirty (30) calendar days, provided the claimant submits a signed statement from a qualified technician describing why the damage was not discoverable at delivery.

B. The January 2024 Shipment

3.6 On or about January 8, 2024, the Department booked a shipment under the Agreement consisting of one (1) Helios 9000 ultra-low-temperature freezer unit, serial number HL9-44117, to be transported from the manufacturer in Port Renfrew to the Coldroom Annex at 1140 Pier Street.

3.7 The bill of lading for the shipment, attached hereto as Exhibit B, states a declared value of twelve thousand dollars ($12,000). The Department did not purchase supplemental declared-value coverage for this shipment.

3.8 Granite's driver, an employee with eleven years of experience and no prior cargo claims, transported the freezer unit and delivered it to the Coldroom Annex loading dock on January 11, 2024, at approximately 9:40 a.m.

3.9 Mr. Kaur, acting on behalf of the Department, signed the delivery receipt at 9:52 a.m. on January 11, 2024. The delivery receipt, attached hereto as Exhibit C, bears the notation "received in apparent good order and condition" and contains no exception, reservation, or notation of damage of any kind.

3.10 Granite's delivery logs, attached hereto as Exhibit D, show that the trailer's refrigeration unit maintained a continuous temperature between 2.1 and 3.4 degrees Celsius throughout transit, well within the range specified for the cargo.

C. The Department's Damage Claim

3.11 On February 2, 2024 — twenty-two (22) calendar days after delivery — the Department sent Granite an email, attached hereto as Exhibit E, asserting for the first time that the freezer unit's compressor had been damaged in transit and demanding payment of thirty-eight thousand five hundred dollars ($38,500), the cost of a replacement compressor and associated labor.

3.12 The February 2 email did not include photographic documentation taken at the time of delivery. The photographs attached to the email were taken on January 30, 2024, according to their embedded metadata, nineteen (19) days after delivery.

3.13 The February 2 email did not include a signed statement from a qualified technician describing why the alleged damage was not discoverable at delivery.

3.14 On February 9, 2024, Granite's claims department responded in writing, attached hereto as Exhibit F, denying the claim on the grounds that: (a) the written claim was not submitted within fourteen (14) calendar days of delivery as required by Section 7.3; (b) the latent-damage exception under Section 7.3(c) did not apply because no qualifying technician statement was provided; and (c) the Department's own delivery receipt noted the cargo was received in apparent good order and condition.

3.15 On February 20, 2024, the Department submitted a supplemental letter, attached hereto as Exhibit G, enclosing a statement from a refrigeration technician, Mr. Sven Nakamura of Saltmarsh Supply's service division, dated February 18, 2024, opining that compressor damage of the type observed "could in some cases" escape detection at delivery.

3.16 The supplemental submission of February 20, 2024, was made forty (40) calendar days after delivery, outside even the extended thirty (30) day period provided by Section 7.3(c) for latent damage claims.

D. The Unpaid Invoices

3.17 Between October 2023 and January 2024, Granite issued the Department six (6) invoices for transport services rendered under the Agreement, as follows:

Invoice G-1041, dated October 6, 2023, in the amount of $4,120.00, received by the Department October 9, 2023;
Invoice G-1058, dated October 27, 2023, in the amount of $6,340.00, received by the Department October 30, 2023;
Invoice G-1072, dated November 14, 2023, in the amount of $3,905.00, received by the Department November 16, 2023;
Invoice G-1090, dated December 5, 2023, in the amount of $7,860.00, received by the Department December 8, 2023;
Invoice G-1103, dated December 19, 2023, in the amount of $5,275.00, received by the Department December 21, 2023;
Invoice G-1119, dated January 9, 2024, in the amount of $8,400.00, received by the Department January 11, 2024.

3.18 The Department paid Invoice G-1041 in full on November 20, 2023, forty-two (42) days after receipt, within the forty-five (45) day period provided by Section 4.2.

3.19 The Department paid Invoice G-1058 in full on December 18, 2023, forty-nine (49) days after receipt, four (4) days beyond the forty-five (45) day period. Granite assessed no interest on this late payment as a courtesy and does not seek interest on Invoice G-1058 in this action.

3.20 The Department has paid no portion of Invoices G-1072, G-1090, G-1103, or G-1119. The total unpaid principal on these four invoices is twenty-five thousand four hundred forty dollars ($25,440.00).

3.21 On March 1, 2024, Granite's accounts receivable department sent the Department a written demand for payment of the four unpaid invoices, attached hereto as Exhibit H. The Department has not responded to the demand.

3.22 Interest under Section 4.4 on the unpaid invoices, calculated through the date of filing, totals two thousand one hundred six dollars and forty cents ($2,106.40), as itemized in the declaration of Granite's controller filed concurrently herewith.

E. The Freezer Unit Retention

3.23 On information and belief, the Department continues to possess and use the Helios 9000 freezer unit at the Coldroom Annex. Photographs taken by a Granite field representative on March 14, 2024, from the public right-of-way on Pier Street, attached hereto as Exhibit I, show the unit visible through the Annex's ground-floor window, powered on, with sample racks installed.

3.24 On March 18, 2024, Dr. Novak sent Granite a letter, attached hereto as Exhibit J, stating that the Department "intends to withhold payment of all outstanding invoices until such time as Granite makes the Department whole on the damaged freezer," and asserting a right of setoff against the invoice balance.

3.25 The Agreement contains no provision authorizing the Department to withhold payment of invoices as a setoff against unadjudicated cargo claims. Section 9.2 of the Agreement expressly provides that "payment obligations under this Agreement shall not be conditioned upon, offset against, or withheld pending resolution of any claim under Section 7."

IV. FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION — BREACH OF CONTRACT

4.1 Granite realleges and incorporates by reference the allegations of paragraphs 1.1 through 3.25 as though fully set forth herein.

4.2 The Agreement is a valid and enforceable contract. Granite has performed all conditions precedent required of it under the Agreement.

4.3 The Department breached Section 4.2 of the Agreement by failing to pay Invoices G-1072, G-1090, G-1103, and G-1119 within forty-five (45) days of receipt.

4.4 As a direct and proximate result of the Department's breach, Granite has suffered damages in the amount of $25,440.00 in unpaid principal, plus contractual interest under Section 4.4 of the Agreement, plus costs of collection as provided in Section 9.6.

V. SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION — UNJUST ENRICHMENT

5.1 Granite realleges and incorporates by reference the allegations of paragraphs 1.1 through 4.4 as though fully set forth herein.

5.2 In the alternative, if the Agreement is found unenforceable in whole or in part, Granite conferred a benefit upon the Department by performing transport services with a reasonable value of $25,440.00, the Department accepted and retained that benefit, and it would be inequitable for the Department to retain the benefit without payment.

VI. THIRD CAUSE OF ACTION — CONVERSION

6.1 Granite realleges and incorporates by reference the allegations of paragraphs 1.1 through 5.2 as though fully set forth herein.

6.2 The replacement compressor purchased by the Department was delivered to the Coldroom Annex on February 26, 2024, by Tidewater Freight, a carrier unaffiliated with Granite. On information and belief, the Department removed the original compressor from the freezer unit and directed Tidewater Freight to haul the original compressor to a salvage facility without notice to Granite, thereby depriving Granite of the opportunity to inspect the allegedly damaged part.

6.3 By disposing of the original compressor, the Department exercised dominion and control over property in which Granite held a contractual inspection right under Section 7.5 of the Agreement, inconsistent with Granite's rights, constituting conversion.

VII. PRAYER FOR RELIEF

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff Granite Logistics, Inc. prays for judgment against Defendants as follows:

A. On the First Cause of Action, damages of $25,440.00, plus contractual interest of $2,106.40 through filing and accruing thereafter at the contractual rate;
B. On the Second Cause of Action, restitution of $25,440.00 in the alternative;
C. On the Third Cause of Action, damages to be proven at trial, including the fair value of the destroyed inspection opportunity;
D. Costs of suit and reasonable attorneys' fees as provided in Section 9.6 of the Agreement;
E. Such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.

DATED this 3rd day of April, 2024.

INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — Harbor Foods, Distribution Center 4
Incident ID: HF-2024-0317
Author: Esi Delgado, Senior Logistics Analyst
Date of report: April 9, 2024

Summary
On March 17, 2024, a scheduled outbound shipment of refrigerated dairy products (order HF-88231, 14 pallets, consignee: regional grocery cooperative) departed Distribution Center 4 approximately nine hours later than its planned departure time of 06:00. The consignee reported spoilage on two pallets upon receipt. This document records the timeline, contributing factors, root cause analysis, and corrective actions.

Timeline (all times local)
05:10 — Outbound dock crew began staging order HF-88231. Staging sheet listed dock door 7.
05:40 — Carrier vehicle (contracted refrigerated trailer, carrier reference CTL-55) arrived and checked in at the gate. Gate log shows the driver was directed to dock door 3, which was occupied by an unrelated inbound load.
06:00 — Planned departure time. Trailer was not yet at a dock.
06:25 — Trailer repositioned to dock door 7 after the inbound load cleared.
06:30–08:15 — Loading proceeded. During loading, the crew discovered that three pallets had been labeled with pick labels for a different order (HF-88219, dry goods) during the previous night's pick shift. The mislabeled pallets had to be returned to the cooler, re-picked, and re-wrapped.
08:15–09:30 — Re-pick and re-wrap completed; loading resumed.
10:40 — Trailer's refrigeration unit was started for pre-cooling. The unit's controller displayed a fault code; the driver reset it, and the unit reached setpoint after approximately 40 minutes.
11:20 — Pre-trip inspection completed; temperature verified at 2°C.
11:45 — Trailer departed the facility.
14:30 — Severe weather advisory issued for the consignee's region; the driver reported heavy rain and reduced speed en route.
March 18, 03:50 — Trailer arrived at consignee. Delivery appointment had been 22:00 on March 17.

Contributing factors considered
1. Gate direction error: the trailer was initially sent to an occupied dock door, costing roughly 45 minutes.
2. Pick-label mismatch: three pallets carried labels for order HF-88219. Root cause analysis (below) attributes the majority of the delay to this event, as re-picking and re-wrapping consumed approximately two hours and forty-five minutes, the largest single block of lost time.
3. Refrigeration unit fault code: delayed pre-cooling by about 40 minutes. Maintenance records show the unit had a similar fault cleared on March 2; the carrier's fleet team has been notified.
4. Weather: heavy rain slowed transit, but the transit delay alone would not have caused the missed appointment had departure been on time.

Root cause
The investigation team concludes that the primary root cause of the late departure was the pick-label mismatch originating in the night pick shift of March 16–17. The label printer at pick station 12 was found to be caching a previous order's label template; a firmware defect in the printer caused it to intermittently reprint cached labels. The gate direction error and the refrigeration fault were secondary contributors.

Impact
Two pallets of yogurt product exceeded their temperature excursion threshold during the extended dwell and transit and were destroyed on receipt. Credit issued to the consignee: $4,180. The remaining twelve pallets were accepted.

Corrective actions
1. Printer firmware at all pick stations to be updated by April 30; interim manual label verification step added to the pick process (owner: warehouse operations).
2. Gate check-in procedure revised: dock assignment to be confirmed against the yard management system before directing any vehicle (owner: gate supervisor).
3. Carrier asked to provide maintenance records for unit CTL-55 and to certify resolution of the recurring fault code (owner: transportation manager).
4. Departure-time buffer for refrigerated loads increased from 30 to 60 minutes pending review.

Lessons learned
Multiple small delays compounded into a missed appointment. The team notes that had any single one of the three mechanical or procedural failures been absent, the shipment would likely have departed within the acceptable window, though this counterfactual does not change the root cause assignment above.

Sign-off: Esi Delgado, Senior Logistics Analyst. Reviewed by the DC4 operations manager, April 11, 2024.

NORTHWIND ANALYTICS — FREIGHT CLAIMS AND RETURNS POLICY (Internal Policy Page, rev. 4.2, effective February 1, 2024)
Owner: Xiu Lindqvist, Director of Supply Chain Operations

1. Purpose
This policy governs the submission, evaluation, and resolution of freight claims and customer return authorizations for all shipments arranged by Northwind Analytics on behalf of its clients.

2. Eligible claim categories
Northwind will accept and process claims in the following categories:
(a) Physical damage to goods discovered at delivery and noted on the delivery receipt at the time of receipt ("visible damage").
(b) Shortage — units missing from a shipment relative to the bill of lading — when the shortage is noted on the delivery receipt at the time of receipt.
(c) Total loss of a shipment in transit, where the carrier confirms non-delivery.
(d) Temperature excursion for shipments moved under a temperature-controlled service level, where the data logger record shows the product exceeded its stated range for more than four (4) consecutive hours.

3. Categories not eligible
Northwind will not process claims for:
(a) Concealed damage discovered after the delivery receipt has been signed without notation.
(b) Damage to goods packaged by the shipper in packaging that fails Northwind's published packaging standard PS-11, as determined by the packaging engineering team.
(c) Delay alone, without associated physical loss or damage, except where a guaranteed-service refund applies under a separate service agreement.
(d) Claims submitted more than sixty (60) days after the delivery date.
(e) Shipments tendered under client-arranged transportation, where the client selected and paid the carrier directly.

4. Submission requirements
All claims must include: the delivery receipt with any notations; photographs of damage where applicable; the commercial invoice value of the affected goods; and, for temperature claims, the complete data logger export. Claims missing required documentation will be pended for up to twenty (20) business days and then closed if documentation is not received.

5. Valuation and limits
Claims are paid at invoice value of the affected goods, capped at $25,000 per shipment unless the client purchased declared-value coverage at tender. Salvage rights belong to Northwind once a claim is paid in full.

6. Return authorizations
Clients may request a return merchandise authorization (RMA) within thirty (30) days of delivery for unopened, saleable goods. Opened or temperature-sensitive goods are not returnable except where a paid damage claim applies. Return freight for client-convenience returns is at the client's expense; return freight for Northwind error is at Northwind's expense.

7. Examples (illustrative only)
Example A: A client reports dented cartons noted on the delivery receipt, submitted 12 days after delivery with photos and invoice — eligible under 2(a).
Example B: A client discovers crushed interior units three weeks after a clean-signed receipt — ineligible under 3(a), notwithstanding the photographs.
Example C: A temperature-controlled shipment whose logger shows a six-hour excursion above range — eligible under 2(d), subject to the logger export.
Example D: A shipment that arrived five days late with goods intact and no guaranteed service purchased — ineligible under 3(c).
Example E: A shortage of 40 units recorded by the consignee on the delivery receipt, claim filed at day 71 — ineligible under 3(d) despite meeting category 2(b).

8. Escalation
Disputes over claim determinations may be escalated to the Director of Supply Chain Operations within fifteen (15) days of the determination letter. The Director's decision is final for claims under $10,000; larger disputes follow the arbitration clause of the master services agreement.

9. Definitions
"Delivery receipt" means the document signed by the consignee at the point of delivery, including electronic proof-of-delivery records. "Clean-signed" means signed without damage or shortage notation. "Data logger" means the calibrated temperature recording device required on all temperature-controlled tenders.

Change history: rev. 4.0 (June 2023) added the four-hour excursion threshold, replacing the prior two-hour threshold; rev. 4.1 (October 2023) added the documentation pending procedure; rev. 4.2 (February 2024) raised the per-shipment cap from $20,000 to $25,000.

INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — Quill Rentals, Regional Shuttle Network
Incident ID: QR-2024-118
Author: Priya Mensah, Network Reliability Lead
Report date: June 3, 2024

Summary
Between May 20 and May 24, 2024, on-time performance on the Quill Rentals regional shuttle network fell to 81%, triggering client escalations from three accounts. This postmortem covers the triggering event, the cascade, contributing factors, and remediation.

Triggering event
On May 20, the Port of Bellingham authority announced an unscheduled closure of Berth 6 for emergency crane repairs. Quill Rentals' cross-dock facility adjacent to Berth 6 handles roughly 40% of the network's inbound container volume. The closure forced diversion of inbound containers to the Port of Tacoma, adding an average of 11 hours of drayage and rail transfer time per container.

Cascade
May 20–21: Fourteen inbound containers were diverted. Cross-dock staffing had been scheduled against the normal Berth 6 arrival pattern; on May 21 the facility operated at approximately 55% utilization while Tacoma arrivals had not yet reached the network.
May 22: Diverted containers began arriving in a compressed window. The cross-dock experienced a 9-hour queue at receiving. Sixteen outbound shuttle departures left late; nine left on time.
May 23: To recover, management authorized rerouting four outbound shuttle runs to a direct line-haul path, bypassing the cross-dock. This recovered schedule for those four runs but stranded two trailer pools at the cross-dock, worsening May 24 departures for the east loop.
May 24: East loop departures ran at 60% on-time. West loop, unaffected by the trailer pool issue, ran at 97% on-time.

Contributing factors assessed
1. Berth closure (external): the initiating event, outside Quill Rentals' control. Force majeure notices were sent to affected clients on May 20, within the contractual 72-hour window.
2. Staffing model rigidity: schedules are fixed 72 hours in advance and could not be flexed to match the diverted arrival pattern. Assessed as the largest internal contributor.
3. Rerouting decision of May 23: recovered four runs but degraded the east loop on May 24. The postmortem review board assessed this decision as reasonable with the information available at the time, but notes that a trailer-pool impact check, which exists in the planning tool but was not run, would have flagged the east loop risk.
4. Communication gap: two of the three escalating clients received proactive notice; the third learned of delays from its consignee. The account team had an outdated escalation contact for that client.

What was not a cause
The review board explicitly considered and ruled out two hypothesized causes: (a) a reported ELD malfunction on vehicle QR-2210 on May 22 was investigated and found to be a display fault with no impact on hours-of-service compliance or routing; (b) a fuel-price surcharge dispute with one carrier partner, resolved May 15, predated the incident and played no role in the week's performance.

Remediation
1. Cross-dock staffing model to include a diversion scenario preset by July 15 (owner: workforce planning).
2. Trailer-pool impact check to be made a mandatory step in the rerouting workflow, enforced by the planning tool rather than by checklist (owner: systems).
3. Escalation contact list to be revalidated quarterly (owner: account management).
4. Diversion playbook for Berth 6 closures to be drafted jointly with the port authority liaison (owner: network operations).

Performance recovery
On-time performance for the week of May 27 recovered to 94%. The review board considers the incident closed as of June 3, 2024, with remediation items tracked separately.

Sign-off: Priya Mensah, Network Reliability Lead.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE - March 1

Harbor Outfitters Partners with Kellerman Polar Studies Lab on 2025 Field Methods Grant

HARBOR CITY - Harbor Outfitters, the expedition gear cooperative, and the Kellerman Polar Studies Lab at Briskett University today opened the fifth annual Field Methods Grant program, which funds graduate researchers who need cold-weather field time more than they need another conference.

'We kept meeting students with solid science and no boots,' said program coordinator Greta Lindqvist. 'This program fixes the boots part, and a fair bit of the science part too.' Two grants of up to $18,000 will be awarded this cycle, same as last year.

Key dates for the 2025 cycle. Applications open thirty (30) days after the date of this announcement. The firm application deadline is April 15; the lab does not read late submissions, full stop. An applicant webinar runs March 20, with a recording posted after. The review panel convenes April 20 to begin scoring the pool. The letter-of-intent workshop is scheduled for April 27, which the lab admits is akward timing for applicants but the room was free. Award recipients will be announced May 12. Funding becomes available on the first day of the second calendar month following the award announcement, which gives the university payroll office time to set up accounts. The equipment depot open house, where winners get fitted for parkas and sleds, is April 18 and is mostly aimed at last years cohort anyway.

Funded teams join the August field school on the Greenland ice margin, August 3-14, travel covered seperately. Applicants must be enrolled graduate students at any accredited university; last years winners are barred from reapplying for one cycle. Letters of recomendation are optional but the panel admits they get read.

About Harbor Outfitters: a member-owned supplier of expedition kit since 1987, proud sponser of 31 field seasons. About the Kellerman Lab: a 14-person research group studying ice-margin hydrology, based at Briskett University.

Media contact: Greta Lindqvist, program coordinator. Posted to the lab news page March 1 at 09:00 local time.

PRESS RELEASE - June 25, 2024

Harbor Supply Completes Microscope Donation to Redding University Optics Lab

REDDING - Harbor Supply, the lab-equipment refurbisher, today marked the close of its donation of a refurbished fluorescence microscope to the Redding University optics teaching lab, capping a project that ran most of the spring semester and a fair bit of last winter too.

The instrument was purchased at auction on March 3, 2022 and sat in Harbor Supply's warehouse while the company sourced a replacement laser module. It was commisioned at Redding on June 10, 2022, the date printed on the acceptance certificate signed by both parties. Harbor Supply's standard warranty covers refubished instruments for 24 months from the commissioning date, not from the purchase date, a clause the company says suprises people every single time.

On June 8, 2024 the lab reported that the focus drive had failed mid-practical. 'Students were queued around the bench when it just stoped,' said lab director Wanjiru Petrov. 'Harbor Supply picked up on the first ring and had a tech out the next morning.' The repair is now complete and the instrument is back in the teaching rotation.

Project phases, per the joint project sheet: site preparation was scheduled to end Febuary 15 and actuallly finished Febuary 12. Installation was scheduled to end April 30 but finished May 6 after a freight elevator breakdown kept the crated instrument in the lobby for a week, which the facilities office would prefer we not mention. Calibration finished May 30. User training was scheduled to end June 20 and finished June 18, with two sessions to spare.

The donation agreement also includes a spare-parts kit, two years of discounted service visits after the warranty lapses, and a promise from the students to stop using the good slides for pratice. Harbor Supply says a second donation, to the chemistry department, is 'in discusion' with no dates set.

Contact: Wanjiru Petrov, lab director, Redding University optics lab. Photos avaliable on request.

BRASSLINE FABRICATION WORKS
COMPANY POLICY AND PROCEDURE MANUAL
Document ID: BFW-QMS-2023-REV-11
Effective Date: January 9, 2023
Supersedes: BFW-QMS-2022-REV-10
Owner: Quality Assurance Department
Approved by: H. Osei, Plant Manager; R. Calloway, Director of Quality

SECTION 1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

1.1 This manual defines the quality management, safety, purchasing, shipping, returns, calibration, and personnel procedures applicable to all operations conducted at Brassline Fabrication Works ("the Company"), a precision machining and light-assembly shop serving customers in the medical-device, aerospace-support, and industrial-equipment sectors.

1.2 The procedures herein apply to all employees, temporary workers, contractors, and interns while on Company premises or performing work on behalf of the Company at customer sites, except where a customer-specific quality agreement expressly supersedes a provision of this manual. In the event of a conflict between this manual and a customer-specific agreement, the customer-specific agreement controls for that customer's work only, and this manual continues to control for all other work.

1.3 Nothing in this manual shall be construed to relieve any employee of obligations imposed by applicable law. Where a provision of this manual is stricter than applicable law, this manual's stricter provision applies. Where applicable law is stricter than this manual, the law applies.

1.4 Department managers may issue local work instructions to supplement this manual. A local work instruction may never weaken a requirement of this manual; it may only add detail or raise the stringency of controls. Any local work instruction that purports to grant an exception to this manual is void unless countersigned by the Director of Quality.

SECTION 2. DEFINITIONS

2.1 "Nonconformance" means any departure from a drawing, specification, purchase order, router, work instruction, or customer requirement, whether discovered before or after delivery.

2.2 "Nonconformance Report" ("NCR") means the documented record of a nonconformance, initiated on Form QF-22, containing the part number, lot number, quantity affected, description of the departure, disposition, and root-cause section where required.

2.3 "Scrap" means material or product determined to be unusable for its intended purpose and not economically reworkable.

2.4 "Rework" means operations performed on nonconforming product to bring it into conformance with the original specification. Work performed to a revised specification approved by the customer is "repair," not rework, and is documented differently.

2.5 "Standard Part" means any part listed in the current published catalog. "Custom Part" means any part manufactured to a customer-supplied drawing or customer-modified catalog drawing. A catalog part that has merely been plated, coated, engraved, or cut to length per customer request is a Custom Part for the purposes of Section 9 (Returns), regardless of the simplicity of the modification.

2.6 "Business Day" means any day the shop is scheduled to operate, Monday through Friday, excluding Company holidays listed in Appendix D.

2.7 "Delivery Date" means the date the carrier records delivery at the customer's receiving dock, not the date the shipment left the Company's dock.

SECTION 3. PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT

3.1 General. The Company provides personal protective equipment ("PPE") at no cost to employees. Employees are responsible for wearing the required PPE in designated areas and for reporting damaged PPE to their supervisor the same day.

3.2 Machining Area. Safety glasses with side shields must be worn by every person within the yellow-lined boundaries of the machining area at all times when any machine in that area is capable of being energized, which for practical purposes means at all times during scheduled operating hours. This requirement is not suspended when machines are idle, during shift changes, during lunch periods, or during cleaning. Visitors, office staff passing through, and vendors are not exempt. The requirement is waived only during a documented full-area lockout/tagout event recorded on Form SF-04, during which all machines in the area are de-energized and locked, and then only for persons participating in or escorted within the scope of that lockout event.

3.3 Grinding and Deburring Station. In addition to safety glasses, a face shield is required whenever grinding or wire-wheel operations are actively in progress. The face-shield requirement attaches to the operation, not the area: a person walking past the grinding station who is not performing grinding or wire-wheel work is not required to wear a face shield, but remains subject to the safety-glasses requirement of Section 3.2.

3.4 Hearing Protection. Hearing protection is required in the press room during press operation and in the tumbling room during tumbling cycles. Sound-level surveys are posted at each door. Hearing protection is not required in the machining area under Section 3.2 unless a posted survey indicates time-weighted average noise at or above 85 dBA, in which case signage will state "HEARING PROTECTION REQUIRED" and that signage controls.

3.5 Footwear. Leather or equivalent closed footwear is required throughout the production floor. Steel-toe footwear is required in the shipping/receiving area and in any area where material over 25 lb is handled, which includes the raw-material rack area and the bar-feed loading positions.

3.6 Gloves. Cut-resistant gloves are required when handling sheet metal, deburred edges, or bar stock. Gloves of any kind are prohibited within arm's reach of rotating spindles, chucks, or exposed rotating tooling. An employee who is handling sharp stock and then intends to operate a lathe must remove the gloves before approaching the spindle; the prohibition on gloves near rotating equipment takes precedence over the cut-resistant glove requirement at the point of machine operation.

3.7 Enforcement. A first PPE violation results in documented coaching. A second violation within twelve months results in a written warning. A third violation within twelve months of the written warning results in suspension without pay for one day and referral to the disciplinary process in Section 14. PPE violations are never waived because the task was of short duration; there is no "quick job" exception anywhere in this section.

SECTION 4. NONCONFORMANCE REPORTING

4.1 Triggering Events. An NCR shall be initiated without delay upon discovery of any of the following:
(a) product received from a customer as a return, whether or not the returned product is ultimately found to be conforming, because the return itself constitutes a report of a suspected nonconformance that must be dispositioned;
(b) internally discovered scrap, whether produced by machining error, handling damage, or material defect, when the scrapped quantity exceeds one piece or when any single piece has a material-and-labor value exceeding $150;
(c) supplier-supplied material or components found to be out of specification at receiving inspection or at any later point, regardless of whether the supplier agrees with the finding;
(d) any out-of-tolerance condition discovered by a customer after delivery, communicated by any channel including telephone, email, or informal conversation, and regardless of whether the customer requests corrective action;
(e) any use of expired, uncalibrated, or suspect measurement equipment in an acceptance decision, upon discovery that the equipment was expired, uncalibrated, or suspect at the time of the acceptance decision.

4.2 Events Not Requiring an NCR. The following do not require an NCR:
(a) a first-piece inspection rejection caught before any production pieces are run, provided the setup is corrected and no suspect product has been produced;
(b) cosmetic blemishes on internal shop aids, fixtures, or tooling that do not contact product;
(c) documentation typos on internal travelers that do not affect traceability, provided the typo is corrected by single-line strikeout, initial, and date;
(d) near-miss safety events with no product involvement — these are recorded on the safety near-miss log under Section 13, not on an NCR, unless product was also affected, in which case both records are required.

4.3 Initiation. Any employee may initiate an NCR; no approval is required to initiate one. An employee who is unsure whether an event requires an NCR shall treat the event as requiring one; erring on the side of initiation is the stated policy, and no employee shall be disciplined for initiating an NCR that is later determined to have been unnecessary.

4.4 Disposition Authority. Dispositions of "use-as-is" on Custom Parts for medical-device customers require written customer concurrence in addition to Quality Engineer approval. Dispositions of "rework" require Quality Engineer approval. Dispositions of "scrap" follow the financial authorization ladder in Section 5. Dispositions of "return to supplier" require Purchasing concurrence.

4.5 Root Cause. An NCR valued over $500 in total impact, or any NCR that is the third or more NCR on the same part number within a rolling six-month window, requires a documented root-cause analysis (5-Why or fishbone) and a corrective-action section. NCRs below both thresholds require disposition only; root-cause analysis for below-threshold NCRs is permitted but not mandatory.

4.6 Timing. NCRs shall be initiated within one Business Day of discovery. Disposition shall occur within five Business Days of initiation for in-house product and within ten Business Days for product requiring customer concurrence. Failure to meet these timing requirements does not invalidate the NCR but is tracked as a quality-system metric reported monthly to the Plant Manager.

4.7 No employee shall close an NCR that they initiated unless they are also the designated disposition authority. Initiation and closure by the same person is prohibited even when that person holds disposition authority for the relevant category; a second qualified person must review and close.

SECTION 5. SCRAP AND FINANCIAL AUTHORIZATION

5.1 Scrap Value Calculation. Scrap value for authorization purposes is the sum of material cost at the most recent purchase price plus accumulated labor at the standard shop rate through the last completed operation. Outside processing costs already incurred (plating, heat treat, coating) are included in scrap value.

5.2 Authorization Ladder. Scrap dispositions are authorized as follows:
(a) value up to and including $500: the shift supervisor may authorize;
(b) value over $500 and up to and including $2,000: the Production Manager must authorize;
(c) value over $2,000 and up to and including $10,000: the Director of Quality must authorize, with the Production Manager concurring;
(d) value over $10,000: the Plant Manager must authorize, with the Director of Quality concurring, and the event must additionally be reported to the ownership group within five Business Days.

5.3 The authorization ladder applies to the total value of a single scrap event, not to the value per piece. Splitting a scrap event into multiple smaller dispositions to remain within a lower authorization tier is a violation of this manual and is treated as a falsification of quality records under Section 14.

5.4 Scrap of customer-owned material follows the same ladder, and the customer must additionally be notified in writing before disposition, except where the customer's quality agreement grants standing disposition authority, in which case notification within five Business Days after disposition satisfies this section.

5.5 Rework Approval. Rework that adds labor cost exceeding $300 per event requires Production Manager approval before the rework begins. Rework discovered after the fact to have exceeded $300 without prior approval does not retroactively become scrap; it is documented as a procedural deviation attached to the NCR.

SECTION 6. CALIBRATION

6.1 All measurement and test equipment used to make acceptance decisions shall be calibrated on the schedule recorded in the calibration database. Calibration intervals range from three to twelve months depending on equipment type and are set by the Quality Engineer.

6.2 Out-of-Calibration Discovery. When equipment is found to be out of calibration, the finding triggers an NCR under Section 4.1(e) for every acceptance decision made with that equipment since its last successful calibration, unless the as-found readings demonstrate the equipment remained within tolerance, in which case the NCR is still initiated but may be dispositioned "no product impact" with the as-found data attached. The presumption is product impact; the burden of demonstrating no impact rests on the Quality department.

6.3 Employees shall not use personal measurement tools for acceptance decisions. Personal tools may be used for operator convenience checks only, and product accepted on the basis of a personal tool is nonconforming product regardless of whether it actually meets specification.

6.4 Calibration labels shall not be removed, covered, or altered. A tool found without a legible calibration label is treated as uncalibrated from the moment of discovery.

SECTION 7. PURCHASING AND SUPPLIER CONTROL

7.1 Approved Supplier List. Production material and outside processing shall be purchased only from suppliers on the Approved Supplier List ("ASL"). Purchasing from a non-listed supplier is prohibited except under the emergency-purchase procedure of Section 7.4.

7.2 Supplier Scorecards. Suppliers are scored quarterly on quality (PPM), on-time delivery, and responsiveness. A supplier falling below 85 points for two consecutive quarters is placed on probation; a supplier on probation for two consecutive quarters is removed from the ASL unless the Director of Quality grants a written extension of one additional quarter. Only one such extension may be granted per supplier per three-year period.

7.3 Receiving Inspection. All production material receives at minimum a visual and documentation review. Dimensional verification at receiving is required for material flagged by the ASL as "inspect on receipt," for material from any supplier on probation, and for first lots from any new supplier. Material certified by a supplier with a certified-dock-to-line status skips dimensional receiving inspection but not the documentation review; dock-to-line status never waives the material certification review.

7.4 Emergency Purchases. An emergency purchase from a non-listed supplier is permitted when a production line is down or a customer commitment is at risk, and only with the written approval of the Production Manager and the Director of Quality. Emergency purchases are limited to a quantity sufficient to cover fourteen calendar days of demand. An emergency purchase does not add the supplier to the ASL; each subsequent purchase from that supplier requires its own emergency authorization until the supplier is qualified under Section 7.5.

7.5 Supplier Qualification. New suppliers are qualified by a questionnaire, a documentation audit, and a first-article evaluation. Medical-device product suppliers additionally require an on-site audit unless they hold a current ISO 13485 certificate, which the Director of Quality may accept in lieu of the on-site audit.

SECTION 8. SHIPPING AND HANDLING

8.1 Packaging. Product shall be packaged per the packaging specification on the router. Where the router is silent, the default packaging standard PKG-STD-01 applies. Customer-specified packaging supersedes both.

8.2 Preservation. Machined steel parts receive rust preventative before packaging unless the part proceeds directly to plating or coating within forty-eight hours, in which case rust preventative is optional but recommended. Aluminum and stainless parts do not require rust preventative.

8.3 Labeling. Every shipping container shall bear a label with the part number, revision, quantity, lot number, and purchase order number. Mixed lots in a single container are prohibited unless the customer has granted written mixed-lot authorization; where authorized, each lot shall be physically segregated within the container and individually bagged and labeled.

8.4 Carrier Selection. The default carrier is the carrier specified in the routing guide maintained by Shipping. Customer-specified carriers on the purchase order supersede the routing guide. Expedite requests by phone must be confirmed in writing (email suffices) before the shipment leaves the dock; a verbal expedite request that is never confirmed in writing does not obligate the Company to expedite charges.

8.5 Export. Export shipments require a review by the designated export-compliance officer before the shipment is released. No shipment to a destination outside the country shall leave the dock without that review, including shipments of samples, returns, and warranty replacements.

8.6 Dock Hours. The receiving dock is staffed 7:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. on Business Days. Deliveries outside those hours are accepted only by prior arrangement with the Shipping Supervisor; carriers arriving unannounced outside dock hours are turned away, and any resulting detention charges are the carrier's responsibility.

SECTION 9. RETURNS AND CUSTOMER CREDITS

9.1 Return Authorization. All returns require a Return Material Authorization ("RMA") number issued before the product is shipped back to the Company. Product received without an RMA number is quarantined and may be refused; issuance of an RMA number is not an admission of nonconformance.

9.2 Request Windows — Standard Parts. For Standard Parts, an RMA request must be submitted within thirty (30) calendar days of the Delivery Date. Standard Parts returned in resalable condition within that window are credited in full less a restocking fee of fifteen percent (15%) of the invoiced price of the returned items. The restocking fee is waived when the return results from a Company error (mis-shipment, wrong part, wrong quantity) or from a confirmed nonconformance; it is not waived for customer over-ordering, customer schedule changes, or customer design changes on Standard Parts.

9.3 Request Windows — Custom Parts. Custom Parts, as defined in Section 2.5, are not returnable for credit except for confirmed nonconformance or Company error. There is no time window during which a Custom Part may be returned for convenience credit, and no restocking-fee arrangement applies to Custom Parts because convenience returns of Custom Parts are not accepted at any price. An RMA request for a Custom Part that cites a nonconformance must be submitted within ninety (90) calendar days of the Delivery Date; requests citing nonconformance submitted after ninety days are evaluated case-by-case by the Director of Quality, whose decision is final.

9.4 Condition. Returned product must be unused and in the original packaging. Product returned in used condition, or product that has been altered, machined, welded, coated, or assembled by the customer after delivery, is not eligible for credit under any circumstance, including confirmed nonconformance, unless the Director of Quality determines that the alteration did not obscure the ability to verify the reported nonconformance.

9.5 Credit Timing. Approved credits are issued within twenty (20) Business Days of receipt and inspection of the returned product. Credit is issued against the original payment method where feasible. Credits over $5,000 require the Plant Manager's signature in addition to the standard credit-memo approval.

9.6 Freight. Return freight for Company error or confirmed nonconformance is the Company's responsibility; the customer is issued a call tag or freight account number. Return freight for convenience returns of Standard Parts is the customer's responsibility, and freight charges on refused or unauthorized returns are not reimbursed.

9.7 Evaluation Upon Receipt. Every returned lot is inspected and recorded on an NCR per Section 4.1(a), even when the return is a convenience return of a conforming Standard Part; in that case the NCR is dispositioned "no product impact — convenience return" and closed without root-cause analysis.

9.8 Disputes. A customer dispute of a credit decision shall be directed in writing to the Quality department within sixty (60) calendar days of the credit decision. Disputes received after sixty days are acknowledged but not re-adjudicated absent new evidence.

SECTION 10. DOCUMENT AND RECORD CONTROL

10.1 Controlled Documents. The current revision of each controlled document is the version in the document-control database. Printed copies are uncontrolled unless stamped "CONTROLLED COPY" in red. Employees shall verify revision currency before using any printed procedure; use of an obsolete revision is a quality-system deviation even if the obsolete revision's content happens to match the current revision, because the deviation lies in the failure to verify.

10.2 Record Retention. Quality records, including NCRs, inspection records, calibration records, and first-article records, are retained for ten (10) years for medical-device product and seven (7) years for all other product. Financial records are retained per the schedule maintained by the Finance department. Records shall not be destroyed before the end of their retention period even when the customer relationship has ended.

10.3 Correction of Records. Corrections to quality records are made by single-line strikeout, initial, and date. Erasures, correction fluid, and overwriting are prohibited. Electronic records are corrected through the revision function of the applicable system; direct database edits are prohibited and are treated as falsification.

10.4 Drawing Revisions. Work shall proceed only to the drawing revision stated on the router. A customer verbal statement that a new revision is forthcoming does not authorize work to the new revision; only a released purchase order amendment or revised drawing in the document-control system authorizes a revision change.

SECTION 11. TRAINING

11.1 New employees complete orientation training before performing independent work. Orientation covers safety, quality basics, and the employee handbook.

11.2 Job-specific training is documented on the training matrix. An employee shall not perform an operation for which they are not signed off on the training matrix except under the direct supervision of a signed-off employee, and product produced under such supervision is inspected 100% until the trainee is signed off.

11.3 Retraining is required after any NCR whose root cause is identified as a training deficiency, and annually for forklift operators, crane operators, and inspectors. Annual retraining is measured from the date of the last completed training, not from the calendar year; an operator trained March 3 of one year must complete retraining on or before March 3 of the following year.

11.4 Training records are quality records for retention purposes under Section 10.2.

SECTION 12. MAINTENANCE

12.1 Preventive maintenance ("PM") is performed per the PM schedule in the maintenance system. PM tasks may be advanced without restriction. PM tasks may be deferred by up to five (5) Business Days with Production Manager approval recorded in the maintenance system; deferral beyond five Business Days requires Plant Manager approval, and no PM task may be deferred more than fifteen (15) Business Days under any circumstance.

12.2 A machine with an overdue PM beyond the approved deferral limits shall be taken out of service until the PM is completed. Operation of a machine with an overdue PM is a reportable quality event, and product produced on such a machine after the overdue date is suspect product requiring an NCR.

12.3 Machine repairs affecting a machine's ability to hold tolerance require a capability verification (first-piece study or equivalent) before the machine returns to production. Cosmetic repairs and repairs to non-tolerance-affecting systems (lights, enclosures, coolant nozzles) do not require capability verification.

SECTION 13. SAFETY AND INCIDENT REPORTING

13.1 Injuries, however minor, shall be reported to the shift supervisor before the end of the shift on which they occur. "Before the end of the shift" is the controlling deadline; reporting the following morning does not satisfy this section for a day-shift injury.

13.2 Near-miss events are recorded on the near-miss log within two Business Days. Near-miss reporting is anonymous if the reporter chooses, and no disciplinary action may be based solely on an anonymous near-miss report.

13.3 Spills. Chemical spills are contained per the spill-response placard at each storage location. Spills exceeding one gallon, and any spill reaching a floor drain regardless of volume, require evacuation of the immediate area and notification of the Safety Coordinator.

13.4 Forklifts. Only licensed operators on the current forklift roster may operate forklifts. The roster is posted at each forklift charging station. Pedestrians have the right of way in all marked walkways; forklift operators shall stop and yield at every walkway crossing, whether or not a pedestrian is visible.

SECTION 14. DISCIPLINE AND RECORD FALSIFICATION

14.1 Falsification of quality records — including signing for inspections not performed, backdating entries, splitting scrap events to evade authorization tiers, and altering calibration labels — is cause for immediate termination.

14.2 The progressive-discipline ladder (coaching, written warning, suspension, termination) applies to procedural violations generally, but it does not apply to falsification, to safety violations involving intentional bypass of guards or interlocks, or to harassment, each of which may proceed directly to termination.

SECTION 15. INTERNAL AUDITS

15.1 Each department is audited at least once per calendar year against this manual. Audit findings are classified as major, minor, or observation. Major findings require a corrective-action plan within ten Business Days of the audit report; minor findings within twenty Business Days; observations carry no mandatory response deadline.

15.2 Audit findings are not disciplinary in nature and shall not be used as the sole basis for discipline; the purpose of the audit program is system improvement.

SECTION 16. VISITOR CONTROL

16.1 Visitors sign in at the front office, receive a visitor badge, and are escorted in production areas at all times. Visitors are subject to the PPE requirements of Section 3 to the same extent as employees.

16.2 Photography in production areas is prohibited without the Plant Manager's written permission, except by customer auditors photographing their own product during an announced audit.

SECTION 17. CUSTOMER-SPECIFIC NOTES — QUOTE AND ORDER PROCESSING

17.1 Quotations are valid for thirty (30) calendar days from the date of the quotation unless the quotation states a different validity period. An expired quotation is not binding on the Company; orders received against an expired quotation are re-quoted at current pricing before acceptance.

17.2 Order acknowledgments are issued within two Business Days of order receipt. The customer shall review the acknowledgment and report discrepancies within five Business Days of the acknowledgment date. An acknowledgment discrepancy reported after five Business Days is evaluated but the Company is not obligated to honor the original purchase order terms where the acknowledgment differed and the five-day review period elapsed without objection.

17.3 Cancellation of orders for Standard Parts is accepted without charge up to the scheduled ship date. Cancellation of orders for Custom Parts is accepted only for work not yet performed: the customer is liable for material purchased, labor expended, and outside processing completed as of the cancellation date, plus a cancellation charge of ten percent (10%) of the remaining unperformed order value.

17.4 Expediters calling for order status shall be directed to Customer Service. Production employees shall not commit to revised delivery dates on the phone; delivery commitments are made only through Customer Service in writing.

SECTION 18. HOUSEKEEPING

18.1 Workstations are cleaned at the end of each shift. Chips are removed from machine beds daily. Aisles are kept clear; material staged in aisles overnight shall be tagged with a staging tag showing the owner and the date, and staged material may remain in an aisle no more than three Business Days.

18.2 Coolant concentration is checked weekly and recorded. Coolant concentration outside the range specified on the coolant placard is corrected before production resumes on that machine.

APPENDIX A. FORMS INDEX
QF-22 Nonconformance Report; SF-04 Lockout Event Record; QF-31 RMA Log; QF-40 Supplier Scorecard; MT-12 PM Deferral Record; TR-07 Training Sign-off.

APPENDIX B. AUTHORIZATION QUICK REFERENCE
Scrap up to $500: shift supervisor. Over $500 to $2,000: Production Manager. Over $2,000 to $10,000: Director of Quality with Production Manager concurrence. Over $10,000: Plant Manager with Director of Quality concurrence plus ownership notification.

APPENDIX C. RESTOCKING AND RETURN SUMMARY
Standard Parts: 30 calendar days from Delivery Date; 15% restocking fee; fee waived for Company error or confirmed nonconformance; never waived for over-ordering or customer schedule changes. Custom Parts (including any catalog part that has been plated, coated, engraved, or cut to length per customer request): not returnable for convenience at any time; nonconformance-based RMA requests within 90 calendar days of Delivery Date; later requests at Director of Quality's discretion. No credit for customer-altered product unless the Director of Quality finds the alteration did not obscure verification.

APPENDIX D. COMPANY HOLIDAYS
The Company observes the following holidays for Business Day calculation: New Year's Day; Memorial Day; Independence Day; Labor Day; Thanksgiving Day and the following Friday; Christmas Eve; Christmas Day. Floating shutdown weeks, when announced, also count as non-Business Days.

APPENDIX E. REVISION HISTORY
Rev 09 (2021): added Section 7.4 emergency purchases.
Rev 10 (2022): changed Standard Part return window from 45 days to 30 days; added 15% restocking fee (previously 10%); added Section 4.7 separation of initiation and closure.
Rev 11 (2023): added Section 5.5 rework cost approval; clarified Custom Part definition to include plated, coated, engraved, and cut-to-length catalog parts; added Section 13.3 spill thresholds; editorial corrections throughout.

END OF MANUAL

questions.instruction: Verify the following statement about this shop's returns policy: a customer may send back a catalog part that was cut to length to their specified dimension within 30 calendar days of delivery and receive credit, subject only to the standard 15% restocking fee. Answer yes if the statement is supported by the policy, no if it is not.
questions.notes: Per 2.5/9.3/App C, cut-to-length catalog parts are Custom Parts; Custom Parts are 'not returnable for convenience at any time', so the 15% fee window never applies.

questions.instruction: Verify the following statement about PPE rules: an office employee crossing the machining area during the lunch period, while no machine is running, is not required to wear safety glasses because the requirement applies only while machines are in operation. Answer yes if the statement is supported by the policy, no if it is not.
questions.notes: 3.2: requirement is 'not suspended when machines are idle, during shift changes, during lunch periods'; only a documented SF-04 lockout waives it.

questions.instruction: According to this policy, certain events always require a Nonconformance Report (NCR) while others are explicitly excluded or handled elsewhere. Select every event below that the policy says must be recorded on an NCR, treating 'an NCR is initiated even if later dispositioned as no impact' as requiring an NCR.

candidates.description: A conforming standard part sent back by a customer simply because they over-ordered. Example: a customer returns ten excess catalog brackets in perfect condition.
Supplier material found out of specification at receiving inspection, even if the supplier disputes the finding. Example: bar stock measuring under the ordered diameter.
Discovery that a micrometer used for acceptance decisions was past its calibration due date. Example: a final-inspection micrometer found two weeks overdue.
A safety near-miss in which no product was involved or damaged. Example: a dropped wrench that nearly struck an operator but touched no parts.
A customer mentions by phone that a delivered part is out of tolerance but asks for no replacement or credit. Example: a casual mention on a status call.
A first-piece inspection rejection caught before any production pieces are run, after which the setup is corrected. Example: the first part off a new setup fails and the offsets are adjusted.

questions.notes: 4.1(a) covers all customer returns incl. convenience (9.7); 4.1(c) supplier defects; 4.1(e)/6.2 calibration; 4.1(d) customer reports any channel. Excluded: near-miss without product (4.2(d)) and first-piece rejection (4.2(a)).

questions.instruction: Under this shop's scrap-authorization rules, identify which individual must authorize the scrapping of a single lot whose total scrap value (material plus accumulated labor) is calculated at $2,400. Select the option that correctly names the required authorizing role for that value.

candidates.description: The shift supervisor on duty may authorize alone. Example: the supervisor signs the scrap ticket at the machine.
The Production Manager must authorize. Example: the scrap ticket routes to the Production Manager's office for signature.
The Director of Quality must authorize, with the Production Manager concurring. Example: both the Quality Director and Production Manager sign the disposition.
The Plant Manager must authorize with the Director of Quality concurring and ownership notified. Example: the scrap is escalated to the plant office and reported to owners.
None of the above: no listed role correctly matches the required authorization for this value. Example: the policy imposes a different or additional requirement than any option states.

questions.notes: 5.2(c): over $2,000 up to $10,000 requires Director of Quality with Production Manager concurrence; $2,400 falls in that tier, and 5.3 forbids splitting to a lower tier.
